item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — 10,000-ton threshold.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons—or any smaller amount—is not prohibited, even if it causes substantial harm. Companies could deliberately cap each operation below the threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Vessel-by-vessel calculation.** The threshold applies to recovery “by a single vessel,” allowing an operator to divide one mining project among multiple vessels, subsidiaries, or contractors so that no vessel exceeds 10,000 tons.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined yearly measurement.** “Per year” does not specify a calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or rolling 12-month period. That ambiguity could permit strategic timing and make violations difficult to prove.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — No aggregation rule.** The bill does not combine the output of affiliated companies, coordinated vessels, remotely operated mining vehicles, or successive vessel operators. Corporate restructuring or vessel transfers could therefore keep nominal recovery below the threshold.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** It is unclear whether minerals count when disturbed, lifted from the seabed, brought to the surface, transferred to another vessel, or landed ashore. Companies could argue that particular collection or transfer activities do not constitute recovery.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth boundary.** Mining at exactly 200 meters, or in shallower seabed areas with similar ecosystems, falls outside subparagraph (A). The bill also does not say how depth is to be measured in areas with tides or uneven terrain.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Uncertain treatment of mixed operations.** The text does not explain how to count resources recovered during an operation that crosses the 200-meter boundary. An operator could dispute whether all, some, or none of the tonnage counts.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Other mineral resources” is undefined.** The phrase leaves uncertainty about which materials qualify and how mixed material, ore, sediment, waste rock, or extracted concentrates should be weighed.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — Undefined “Secretary.”** The bill never identifies which Cabinet secretary may determine that other activities pose comparable risks. That omission could prevent implementation or invite challenges to any determination.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — No procedure for risk determinations.** The bill supplies no evidentiary standard, rulemaking process, notice requirement, deadline, or judicial-review framework for determining “comparable” risk. It is also unclear whether a determination may apply retroactively to conduct already underway.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — Vague comparison standard.** “Risks … comparable” does not identify which risks, probability, magnitude, geographic scale, or time horizon must be compared. Regulated parties could challenge the standard as insufficiently definite, particularly in a criminal case.

12. **Section 2(2) — Incomplete definition of U.S. person.** The definition omits permanent residents, partnerships, limited liability companies that are not treated as corporations, trusts, associations, and possibly entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or tribal law.

13. **Section 2(2) — Foreign-subsidiary loophole.** A foreign-organized subsidiary of a U.S. company is not itself a “U.S. person,” even when wholly controlled from the United States. Companies could move overseas operations into such entities, subject only to the uncertain reach of the phrase “engage in.”

14. **Section 2(2) — No ownership or control rule.** The bill does not attribute a foreign affiliate’s conduct to its U.S. parent, beneficial owners, officers, or controlling persons. It likewise contains no anti-evasion provision addressing nominal foreign ownership.

15. **Section 2(3) — Registry excludes smaller vessels.** A vessel of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less is not a covered vessel and need not register, even though it might conduct mining prohibited by section 3.

16. **Section 2(3) — “Equipped for” is uncertain.** The bill does not specify what equipment makes a vessel capable of recovery or whether removable equipment, remotely operated vehicles, or support vessels count. Equipment could potentially be installed after registration would otherwise be required.

17. **Section 2(3) — Gross-tonnage standard unspecified.** “Gross tons” can be calculated under different domestic and international systems, but the bill does not designate one. Operators near the cutoff could contest whether their vessels are covered.

18. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the prohibition reaches financing, investment, permitting, equipment sales, technical assistance, processing, transportation, purchasing, or directing a mining venture. Conduct ancillary to physical recovery may therefore remain lawful or be difficult to prosecute.

19. **Section 3(a) — Foreign actors remain largely outside the prohibition.** A foreign person operating outside the United States is not covered. The bill also does not ban importing, buying, processing, or using minerals recovered abroad by such a person.

20. **Section 3(a) — Geographic scope is uncertain.** “Any person in the United States” could refer to the person’s location or the location of the conduct, and “United States” is not defined to include territories, territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, or U.S.-flagged vessels.

21. **Section 3(a) — No attempt, conspiracy, aiding, or evasion language.** The bill expressly prohibits only engaging in completed commercial mining. Preparatory conduct and deliberate assistance could escape civil liability unless another body of law supplies a basis for liability.

22. **Section 3(a) — Threshold delays enforceability.** Because an operation does not fall under section 2(1)(A) until it exceeds 10,000 tons in a year, the government may be unable to stop it prospectively before that point. The bill does not expressly authorize an injunction based on an expected exceedance.

23. **Section 3(b) — Broad grandfather clause.** Mining “conducted under” any exploration license issued before enactment is exempt, with no limit on tonnage, duration, geographic area, environmental effects, or transition period.

24. **Section 3(b) — License issuer is unspecified.** The exemption does not say that the license must have been issued by the United States, the International Seabed Authority, or another recognized regulator. A company could invoke a foreign, subnational, or otherwise questionable pre-enactment license.

25. **Section 3(b) — Exploration licenses may shield commercial mining.** The provision expressly exempts “mining” under an “exploration” license without defining when exploration becomes exploitation. That mismatch could permit large-scale commercial recovery to be characterized as exploration.

26. **Section 3(b) — Transfers and amendments are unaddressed.** The bill does not say whether a grandfathered license may be sold, renewed, extended, expanded, or materially amended after enactment while retaining the exemption.

27. **Section 3(c) — Unlimited environmental-assessment exemption.** The exception has no tonnage cap, duration limit, scientific protocol, permit requirement, independent oversight, or prohibition on selling recovered minerals. A commercial operation could claim that its activities also gather environmental data.

28. **Section 3(c) — Subjective purpose test.** “For the purpose of” does not address mixed-purpose operations or specify whose purpose controls. Proving that an asserted research purpose is pretextual could be difficult.

29. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, chartering, management, and physical operation may be divided among different entities, leaving uncertainty about who must register and report.

30. **Section 4(a) — No registration deadline or pre-operation requirement.** The section does not state when registration must occur or prohibit a vessel from operating while unregistered. It also supplies no mechanism for denying, suspending, or revoking a registration.

31. **Section 4 — Registry is poorly matched to the prohibition.** Registration applies only to large, specially equipped vessels, while section 3 can apply to mining by other means. Conversely, registering a vessel does not itself impose operational conditions or establish that its activities are lawful.

32. **Section 4(b) — Reporting requirements are underspecified.** The bill gives no due dates, required data fields, measurement methods, record-retention rules, audit standards, or treatment of incomplete or amended reports. “Describing” recovery activities could be satisfied by a report too general to support enforcement.

33. **Sections 4 and 5 — No penalty for registry or reporting violations.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failure to register, failure to report, and false or misleading reports are not made violations of this Act, although other generally applicable laws might sometimes apply.

34. **Sections 3–5 — No designated enforcement authority.** The bill does not identify an agency authorized to investigate violations, issue subpoenas, inspect vessels, compel records, bring administrative cases, or seek injunctions. It also does not state who assesses or collects civil penalties.

35. **Section 5(a) — Civil-penalty procedure is absent.** There are no standards for calculating the penalty, notice-and-hearing provisions, limitations period, venue rules, or express authority for judicial enforcement. “Not more than” $1 million also permits a nominal or zero assessment without stated factors.

36. **Section 5(a) — Daily violation is unclear.** The bill does not define when a violation begins or ends, particularly for intermittent recovery, voyages spanning multiple days, or conduct that crosses the annual threshold only late in the year.

37. **Section 5(b) — Criminal provision inherits vague terms.** Although “willfully” provides some protection, criminal liability still depends on uncertain concepts such as “engage in,” “recovery,” “per year,” and “comparable” ecosystem risk. Those ambiguities could be construed narrowly under the rule of lenity.

38. **Sections 5(a) and 8 — Conflicting timing language.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, but section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. The better reading may be that section 3 is not enforceable during that interval, but the inconsistency invites litigation.

39. **Section 6 — International-negotiation duty is weak.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires effort rather than an agreement or even formal negotiations, and it has no reporting requirement or consequence for noncompliance. “Equivalent” prohibitions is also undefined.

40. **Section 7(a) — No process for the National Academies report.** The bill does not require, fund, commission, or set a deadline for the report, and does not specify what subjects or evidence it must address.

41. **Section 7(a) — “Without serious harm” is undefined.** The bill gives Congress no benchmark for what counts as serious harm, over what area or time period, or at what level of scientific certainty. The phrase may create political uncertainty, although Congress remains free to legislate regardless.

42. **Section 7(a) — Ambiguous joint-resolution mechanism.** The bill supplies no expedited procedure, required text, referral rules, or deadline for the contemplated joint resolution. “Acting on” the Academies’ report is also vague and may be difficult to verify or enforce.

43. **Section 7 — Internal duration problem.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress makes the specified finding, but section 7(b) terminates the entire Act after ten years whether or not that finding occurs. The sunset therefore provides an automatic route for mining to resume without any scientific finding.

44. **Section 7(b) — Sunset may disrupt enforcement.** The bill contains no savings clause preserving accrued penalties, pending cases, reporting records, or investigations after the ten-year expiration. Defendants could argue that termination of the Act extinguishes unresolved liabilities or remedies.

45. **Act as a whole — No import, possession, or market restriction.** Even while domestic and U.S.-person mining is prohibited, the bill does not restrict commerce in seabed minerals recovered by uncovered foreign operators. Continued U.S. demand could therefore support the same mining abroad.

46. **Act as a whole — No monitoring or traceability system.** There are no vessel-tracking, observer, landing declaration, mineral-origin, inspection, or recordkeeping requirements beyond self-certified quarterly reports from registered vessels. Operations outside that registry could be difficult to detect and prove.
